actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: The world's largest frog is known only from south-western Cameroon from the region of Nkongsamba, and south to Monte Alen in mainland Equatorial Guinea. In Nkongsamba, it is known from Ekomtolo, Badjong, Mangamba, Nkeba river around Babong, Dibang and the Dibombe river, extending further south to Yabassi, Eseka, Bipindi, Lolodorf, Akom II and Camp-Ma'an (N. Gonwouo pers. comm November 2016). Its presence in Gabon is uncertain. It is generally found at low to medium altitudes, below 1,000 m asl. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 79,839 km<sup>2</sup>.
documentation.population: Due to continued consumption and decline in the extent and quality of habitat, the population is decreasing. This species has decreased significantly as a result of harvesting for food in the past, and this is continues to be a problem today based on researcher observations and interviews with frog hunters (M.-O. Rödel pers. comm. July 2016, N. Gonwouo pers. comm. November 2016). Frog hunters throughout this species' range have reported that subpopulations have reduced and larger individuals are becoming increasingly difficult to find, particularly around villages where it is collected for food (N. Gonwouo pers. comm. November 2016). In 2011, in Ebo Forest this species was only found after 8 hours of walking from the forest edge and it was not common when it was located (M.-O. Rödel pers. comm. July 2016). It was reported that in two weeks of searching, three individuals were encountered, and the species had completely disappeared around villages in this area (M.-O. Rödel pers. comm. July 2016). Surveys were carried out around the Nkongsamba region during the dry season in early 2016 and in Dibang Eseka in July-August 2016 which all recorded this species (N. Gonwouo pers. comm. November 2016). Juveniles are still being found in scanty subpopulations, with the presence of these individuals attributed to migration and recolonization from subpopulations within intact forest, where there is less hunting and the species can still reproduce (N. Gonwouo pers. comm. January 2018). Based on this information, it is estimated that at least 70% of the population has declined over the last 15 years (three generation lengths of this species). Studies are ongoing to determine which of its known localities it has now disappeared from (N. Gonwouo pers. comm. November 2016), with some sites being monitored on an annual basis (N. Gonwouo pers. comm. February 2017).
documentation.habitats:
This species lives in or near fast-flowing rivers and streams in rainforest, preferring warmer, slower rivers than Conraua robusta but faster rivers than C. crassipes. It can survive in secondary habitats close to rivers, as well as in forest, but not in very heavily degraded areas (farm bush). It requires large, clean rivers and, due to the heavy consumption of this species, it is now only found deep in undisturbed forest away from villages (M.-O. Rödel pers. comm. July 2016). Breeding occurs in streams and small rivers. The young rest by flowing water during the day. Around Nkongsamba in western Cameroon, C. goliath, C. crassipes and C. robusta occur sympatrically.

A generation is assumed to be approximately five years.
documentation.threats:
The major threat to this species is hunting for human consumption, both for local subsistence and to be sold at bush meat markets (N. Gonwouo pers. comm. November 2016). New, sophisticated traps for catching this species are now being used in the Nkongsamba area of Cameroon. Large scale collection for the international pet trade is growing and also contributing to the decline of this species (N. Gonwouo pers. comm. November 2016), with animals imported from Cameroon to the USA on a regular basis by animal dealers for zoos, the pet trade and, in the past, for competitive frog races (one estimate of this trade was 300 animals per year). There has been at least one instance of an import into Europe that did not satisfy legal requirements leading to customs seizure (T. Doherty-Bone pers. comm. November 2018).

It is also adversely affected by the loss of forest habitat for agriculture (including the creation of new cocoa plantations, banana plantations, and palm plantations), logging and human settlements. With the creation of a new roads network to extract and commercialise products from these plantations, the habitat of this species is now more accessible to people (N. Gonwouo pers. comm. January 2018). Other threats to its habitat include sedimentation of its breeding streams and the dumping of chemicals in river tributaries by locals often in streams around farms and villages (N. Gonwouo pers. comm. February 2017) where the species reproduces, which is likely to affect tadpole development (N. Gonwouo pers. comm. November 2016).
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions
This species presumably occurs in several protected areas, and is confirmed from Monte Alen National Park in Equatorial Guinea. 

Conservation Needed
Measures are needed to work with local communities to manage the harvest at sustainable levels. A captive-breeding programme should also be considered.

Research Needed
Further data on what might constitute sustainable harvest is needed, as well as the socio-economic drivers of illegal hunting (T. Doherty-Bone pers. comm. November 2018). Actual impact of changes to water quality and riparian vegetation should also be a priority, particularly changes in discharge and agrochemical exposure (T. Doherty-Bone pers. comm. November 2018). Susceptibility to amphibian chytrid fungus (Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis) has not been fully assessed, and given the findings that this pathogen may have a recent Asian origin (O’Hanlon et al. 2018), its novelty to Africa could result in a more substantial threat than previously anticipated.
documentation.use_trade: This species is part of the Central African bushmeat trade and there is large scale collection for the international pet trade (N. Gonwouo pers. comm. November 2016).
documentation.rationale: Listed as Endangered because this species is believed to have declined by >70% over three generations (15 years), based on a reduction in the number of mature individuals due to over-harvesting. This decline is based on the fact that in many places it is necessary to walk between three to five hours from the forest edge to find full adult species (including large individuals), whereas it could be found within one hour’s walk of villages 15 years ago.
